questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the purpose the Declaration gave for declaring separation
questions.stem: In the design brief for the civic pavilion, the architect wants to explain why the Declaration of Independence mattered beyond announcing separation from Britain. Which purpose best fits the document's own framing?

options.text: It created a permanent three-branch government with written powers
options.misconception: treats the declaration as a working constitution

options.text: It negotiated the trade terms that followed the war for independence
options.misconception: confuses political separation with commercial settlement

options.text: It justified separation by appealing to equality and natural rights
It abolished slavery by granting equal legal standing to every colonist
options.misconception: overreads the equality language as reaching slavery

questions.explanation: The Declaration framed the break as a claim about rights and equality, and later reformers reused its language. It neither organized a government nor addressed slavery directly.
questions.hint: Ask what the document itself says it is doing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the structural weakness of the confederation
questions.stem: In a design brief for a national materials consortium, the architect compares the confederation's structural weakness. Which defect best explains its inability to tax or regulate commerce?

options.text: It prohibited the states from levying their own taxes
options.misconception: confuses state sovereignty with a federal prohibition

options.text: It gave the central congress no power to enforce its own resolutions
It made every major action require the votes of all thirteen states
options.misconception: overstates unanimity, which applied to Senate suffrage alone

options.text: It placed the treasury permanently under a foreign accounting body
options.misconception: invents a foreign supervisory body that never existed

questions.explanation: The central congress could request money and pass rules but could not compel states to obey them, so its measures had no effective force. The tempting wrong idea is that the confederation was weak only because states disliked each other.
questions.hint: Focus on whether the center could compel obedience.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a two-chamber proposal for the Great Compromise

stimulus.body: A design studio proposes a building with two chambers: a wide chamber whose members are chosen by population and a smaller chamber whose members are chosen equally by each state. The studio argues the split prevents the smaller states from being overwhelmed by populous ones while still allowing broad representation. A historian objects that the arrangement also created a new veto point for the smallest states.

questions.stem: Given the studio's proposal, which feature of the Great Compromise does the historian's objection best capture?

options.text: It protected small states by making equal state representation a condition of lawmaking
It removed the older objection that a confederation lacked a national government
options.misconception: confuses the structural bargain with the confederation's earlier weakness

options.text: It created a House whose members serve two-year terms in rotation
options.misconception: imports a later tenure rule into the settlement of 1787

options.text: It gave the national legislature the power to tax the states directly
options.misconception: misstates the taxing power, which applied to private goods

questions.explanation: The bargain gave small states a guaranteed share in one chamber, so lawmaking always required their assent as well as majority support. The tempting wrong idea is that the second chamber merely doubled the number of votes.
questions.hint: Ask what the equal-voice chamber could block.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rationale for dividing national authority
questions.stem: In the design brief for a courthouse annex, the architect explains why legislative, executive, and judicial duties were placed in separate hands. Which rationale best fits?

options.text: So that each branch could specialize in the work it was best suited to perform
options.misconception: treats division of labour as the main design goal

options.text: So that no single branch could be accused of acting without broad support
options.misconception: mistakes mutual checks for a requirement of joint action

options.text: So that state governments would keep enough authority to balance the nation
options.misconception: confuses separation of powers with federalism

options.text: So that concentrated power in one branch would invite abuse and self-protection

questions.explanation: The framers feared that a body which made, enforced, and interpreted law could protect itself from correction. The tempting wrong idea is that the split was mainly an efficiency device for dividing routine work.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when one branch holds every power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe how checks and balances restrain concentrated power
questions.stem: In the design brief for a civic center, the architect explains what checks and balances accomplish when one branch tries to exceed its share of power.

answer.exemplar: Checks and balances work by giving each branch specific legal tools to restrain the others: the legislature can refuse money or refuse consent, the executive can veto and the Senate can override, and the courts can declare acts unconstitutional. No branch can enlarge its own powers without the permission of another, so the design depends on rivals with independent authority rather than on good intentions alone.

questions.explanation: Each branch holds legal tools to restrain the others, so no single branch can dominate. The tempting wrong idea is that the branches only divide labour and cannot interfere with each other.
questions.hint: Name one restraining tool for each branch.

questions.stem: In a design brief for a regional water authority, the architect describes a system in which national law applies throughout and state law also applies. Which term names that arrangement?

options.text: A confederation, in which the states hold the real power and the center merely coordinates
options.misconception: chooses confederation for a system with an operative national government

options.text: Federalism, in which national and state governments divide authority and both remain operative
A unitary system, in which all authority flows from a single central government
options.misconception: ignores the constitutionally separate state governments

options.text: A compact, in which the states pledge to each other rather than to a national government
options.misconception: confuses a federal system with an interstate pact

questions.explanation: Federalism keeps two levels of government, each with powers the other cannot simply take, and both make law directly. The tempting wrong idea is that any arrangement with a national center is unitary.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state governments still make and enforce law.

options.text: Because the national list of powers is broad, any state program not listed there must be national
options.misconception: treats silence in the national list as national authority

options.text: Because states held power before the national government existed, state programs are always invalid
options.misconception: confuses inherited state authority with automatic invalidity

options.text: Powers not granted to the national government remain with the states or the people
Because the people are the source of authority, national programs require a direct popular vote
options.misconception: substitutes a voting rule for the reserved-powers rule

questions.explanation: The constitution grants the national government a listed set of powers and no others, so everything else stays with the states or the people. The tempting wrong idea is that an unlisted subject automatically becomes national.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the supremacy rule to conflicting laws
questions.stem: In a design brief for a national compliance system, the architect explains what happens when a state rule conflicts with a valid national law. Which rule governs?

options.text: The valid national law controls, and the conflicting state rule is set aside
The state rule controls because state governments are closer to the affected people
options.misconception: lets proximity to citizens override the constitutional order

options.text: Both rules apply, and the more restrictive one is enforced against everyone
options.misconception: invents a stricter-standard rule with no basis in the text

options.text: The conflict goes to a national vote in which the states decide by majority
options.misconception: invents a referendum mechanism for supremacy conflicts

questions.explanation: The constitution declares itself the supreme law, so a valid national statute displaces a contrary state rule. The tempting wrong idea is that federalism lets a state nullify national law by disagreeing with it.
questions.hint: Ask which law the text declares higher.

options.text: A direct democracy, because assemblies had always produced mob rule
options.misconception: confuses criticism of factions with fear of direct rule

questions.explanation: The framers' central fear was the concentration of power, whichever label attached to the office holding it. The tempting wrong idea is that they were simply nostalgic for monarchy's limits.
questions.hint: Look for the common danger behind the two forms.

options.misconception: reduces the debate to an aimless division of power

That national authority should rest entirely with the states on a permanent basis
options.misconception: substitutes the confederation question for the divided-power debate

options.misconception: confuses the 1776 text with later amendment proposals

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the confederation's amendment rule
questions.stem: The engineering review board asks how the confederation's amendment rule shaped later constitutional design. What does that rule reveal?

options.text: That amendments were thought to be nearly impossible to pass in the first place
options.misconception: assumes unanimity meant amendment was considered impossible

options.text: That the framers wanted all constitutional change to happen without ratification
options.misconception: ignores the ratification requirement entirely

options.text: That the confederation required no consent of the states for any legal change
options.misconception: inverts the rule, which required state consent

options.text: That the unanimity hurdle exposed the need for a more workable amendment path

questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about the compromise from a source

stimulus.body: A regional authority memo argues that the two-chamber design of the national legislature was a compromise between large and small states rather than a compromise between whole nations. questions.stem: Which conclusion about the Great Compromise does the memo's own evidence support?

options.text: The compromise rewarded populous states at the expense of the small ones
options.misconception: reads the population-based chamber as if it were the only chamber

options.text: The compromise created a bicameral legislature without any real dispute to settle
options.misconception: assumes there was no genuine conflict to resolve

options.text: The compromise gave each state veto power over the entire national legislature
options.misconception: upgrades equal representation into a general veto over all lawmaking

options.text: Each state received guarantees in one chamber and population weight in the other

questions.explanation: Population-based representation and equal state representation each protected one side's interest, so neither interest was wholly defeated. The tempting wrong idea is that equal representation made the small states masters of the legislature.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how branches were expected to relate to each other
questions.stem: A civic auditorium's program pairs a speaker on the judiciary with one on the legislature. Which statement best captures how the framers expected the branches to relate?

options.text: Each branch was to act independently with no accountability to the others
options.misconception: confuses separation with an absence of checks

options.text: Each branch was to check the others rather than act as one combined authority
The legislature was to supervise the other branches at every step of their work
options.misconception: reduces separation to legislative supremacy

options.text: The judiciary was to settle every dispute before any other branch acted
options.misconception: makes the judiciary a prior stage rather than a coequal branch

questions.explanation: Separation was meant to be reciprocal: each branch could restrain the others and could itself be restrained. The tempting wrong idea is that the branches were isolated rather than mutually answerable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the restraint runs one way or both.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare modern checks with an older restraint device
questions.stem: A design review asks the panel to compare checks and balances with the older idea that a legislature could restrain a ruler by refusing to fund him.

answer.exemplar: Checks and balances go further than the older refusal-of-supplies idea because restraint is distributed among all three branches rather than concentrated in one. The legislature can refuse appropriations and withhold consent, the executive can veto and be checked by an override, and the judiciary can refuse to enforce an unconstitutional law. Each branch must therefore expect to be judged by the others, which was the point of the arrangement.

questions.explanation: Unlike the older device, each branch in the new design can restrain and be restrained, so power is checked in both directions. The tempting wrong idea is that only the legislature checks the other branches.
questions.hint: Compare the number of branches that can restrain.

questions.explanation: Federalism operates as a shared system: the national level frames the rules and the states carry them out and add detail. The tempting wrong idea is that one level does everything on a given subject.

options.text: Whether the program conflicts with a federal statute on interstate commerce
options.misconception: confuses preemption with the scope of reserved powers

Whether the local authority holds the power only when a federal waiver is absent
options.misconception: invents a waiver requirement for ordinary local powers

questions.explanation: State authority continues until the national government claims the subject, so the classifier asks about the national claim. The tempting wrong idea is that a local program needs a federal waiver to be valid.

options.misconception: assumes states may nullify national requirements

options.text: The stricter state rule may still operate where it does not obstruct the national rule

options.misconception: treats a conflict as cancelling both rules

options.text: The national rule applies only in states that consented to the national system
options.misconception: invents state-by-state consent to national law

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the intended effect of the veto
questions.stem: An engineer's analogy explains a veto as a design feature rather than an obstacle. Which effect did the designers most intend by including it?

answer.exemplar: The veto was meant to force reconsideration rather than to grant permanent superiority to the executive. It gives the executive a chance to object to a law and requires the legislature to act again, with an override route available when the objection is rejected. In this way the device adds friction, delay, and public visibility to the lawmaking process so that no single chamber can quietly dominate the other.

questions.explanation: The veto made lawmaking a two-stage public process, giving the executive a review and the legislature a chance to reconsider. The tempting wrong idea is that the veto let the executive rewrite legislation.
questions.hint: Think about the second look the device forces.

questions.stem: In the design brief for a courthouse, the architect explains why an override vote is worth building into a system with a veto.

answer.exemplar: The override keeps the veto from becoming a final and unanswerable obstacle. answer.exemplar: Each branch is checked by instruments that belong to the others: impeachment and removal for executive misconduct, legislative refusal of appropriations and consent, Senate confirmation of appointments and treaties, veto and override, and judicial review of laws and executive acts. options.misconception: treats constitutional silence as voiding both rules

questions.explanation: A state rule that merely runs alongside a national rule is not displaced; only obstruction triggers supremacy. The tempting wrong idea is that overlapping subject matter alone voids the state rule.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state rule gets in the way.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the warning about preserving republican form
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief for the town hall records the warning that a republic must be kept in due order to preserve its form. What does that warning target?

options.text: The possibility that state governments might decline to cooperate with national laws
options.misconception: redirects the warning toward federalism rather than republics

options.text: The risk that the national judiciary would grow too powerful to check the other branches
options.misconception: redirects the warning toward judicial supremacy

options.text: The danger that voting rules might exclude too many qualified citizens
options.misconception: redirects the warning toward suffrage rules

options.text: The risk that the people might surrender the habits that self-government requires

questions.explanation: The warning concerned popular self-rule: a republic needs citizens who continue to think and act as free participants. The tempting wrong idea is that the warning was aimed at state cooperation.
questions.hint: Ask who could let a republic decay.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Summarize what the constitutional settlement decided about divided power
questions.stem: A closing design note asks what the constitutional settlement of 1787 ultimately decided about divided power. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: National power was divided among branches, with enumerated national powers and reserved state powers
National power was kept whole, with the legislature exercising all national authority
options.misconception: describes the unitary option that was rejected

options.text: National power was left to the states, with no lasting national structure created
options.misconception: describes the confederation that was replaced

options.text: National power was divided permanently, with no mechanism for resolving conflicts among branches
options.misconception: ignores the checks and balances that the settlement created

questions.explanation: The settlement split national power among branches, limited the national government to enumerated powers, and reserved the rest to the states. The tempting wrong idea is that it left the division of power without any means of resolving conflict.
questions.hint: Ask what the settlement limited and what it divided.
